reading.body:
Delaware's 2025, 2026 legislative session treats data centers as a land use and energy problem, not a technology one. Two bills filed on the same day, SB312 on data centers and HB233 on large energy use facilities, address the physical footprint and the power draw as separate statutory subjects. SB353 goes further and proposes a moratorium on data center development. The state is legislating the building and the load, which is where the binding constraint on AI actually sits.

The AI-specific bills are thinner and later. HB16 amends the Artificial Intelligence Commission, HJR7 directs that commission toward a regulatory sandbox for agentic AI, and HB404 creates a schools pilot for AI and extended reality. These are institutional and educational measures. None of them governs compute, siting, or interconnection. The pattern is a state that has separated the governance of AI applications from the governance of the infrastructure AI runs on.

Privacy and data bills run alongside: HB380 on personal data, HB60 on DMV data, HB453 on surveillance-based pricing, HCR20 on student data. SCR18 creates a task force to study nuclear energy. That is the closest the list comes to generation supply, and it is a study, not a mandate.

What this data does not show is outcome. These are bill titles and dates, not enacted law, and the list carries no vote counts, committee actions, or effective dates. It also does not say how much data center capacity Delaware hosts, how much power it draws, or whether any of these measures passed. The reader should treat the volume of activity as a signal of political attention, not of settled policy.
